<reason>Side B won decisively by building a coherent asymmetric-information case and systematically dismantling Side A's economic and practical objections. Side B effectively turned Side A's "stigma" argument into the exact market incentive that compels landlords to make relatively cheap fixes (such as installing parcel lockers or shutting down rogue short-term rentals) rather than suffer rent discounts. Furthermore, Side B exposed multiple contradictions in Side A's case—most notably forcing Side A to walk back its claim that landlords would raise rents to offset a "problem building" discount—and showed that code enforcement and upfront disclosure are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Side A also lost credibility in Pressure Questions [A3.2] by citing its own earlier argument [A2.1] as if it were a concession made by Side B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's dismantling of Side A's claim in [A2.3] that landlords would "raise rents to offset the 'problem building' discount." Using Pressure Question [B3.2] and Rebuttal 2 [B4.5-B4.6], Side B forced Side A to retract the claim as "imprecise" in [A4.2] and pivot to arguing that landlords would raise rents across the rest of their portfolio—a pivot Side B cleanly neutralized in [B5.3] by pointing out that landlords already charge what the market bears elsewhere, leaving actual repair as the only profitable way to eliminate the defect discount.</best_rebuttal>
